intro: The first violin strides into C major, then Haydn stops all four players in their tracks. The Danish String Quartet plays a movement whose silences are as pointed as its running notes.

sections.label: A · C major, interrupted by silence
sections.mNote: The first violin’s bold phrase breaks off repeatedly

sections.label: Dev · The violin phrase starts travelling
sections.mNote: The opening returns loudly over changed chords

sections.label: A′ · C major and the opening phrase
sections.mNote: The cello’s A♭ returns beneath the first violin

cues.title: Four players stop short
cues.text: The first violin throws out a bold phrase above held notes. Then everyone stops. Haydn writes five-bar phrases and pauses for the whole quartet; even the silences refuse to fall into a comfortable four-square pattern.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, Vivace, opening page. Laurie Shulman identifies irregular five-bar phrases and dramatic pauses: https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A violinist goes into business
cues.text: Johann Tost leaves the Esterházy orchestra in 1788 and takes six new Haydn quartets to Paris. These include Op. 54. He arranges their publication with Sieber; his name stays attached to the music.
cues.evidence: Laurie Shulman, programme note, p. 2: Tost’s departure, Paris visit and publication arrangements for Opp. 54 and 55. https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf

cues.title: The violin starts again
cues.text: The quiet close in G major is followed by a loud new statement of the first violin’s opening phrase. The lower strings change the chords beneath it, and the development sends the familiar figure off through new keys.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, Vivace, end of exposition and opening of development, pp. 182–184. Peter Holman discusses the movement’s sharp changes of key: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/notes/66971-B.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: C major, with its shadow
cues.text: The first violin recovers its opening phrase in C major. The cello’s A♭ returns too, colouring the phrase just as it did at the start. Haydn brings back the interruption along with the tune.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, Vivace: opening and recapitulation, including the A♭ bass beneath the restated phrase.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The gentle tune comes home
cues.text: The second-group tune, marked piano dolce, returns in C major. Its lilting phrases provide a softer answer to the first violin’s opening declaration.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, Vivace: the p dolce second group in G major and its C major return.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A quiet close, then a loud restart
transitions.from: A · C major, interrupted by silence
transitions.to: Dev · The violin phrase starts travelling
transitions.how: The exposition closes quietly in G major. The first violin restarts its opening phrase forte over sustained lower strings, with altered notes in the accompaniment pulling it away from G. Haydn puts the bold opening back on stage before allowing it to settle in a key.
transitions.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, Vivace, end of exposition and opening of development.

transitions.title: The cello leads back to C
transitions.from: Dev · The violin phrase starts travelling
transitions.to: A′ · C major and the opening phrase
transitions.how: The bass settles on G before the first violin brings back the opening phrase in C major. A few bars later the cello moves to A♭, restoring the unexpected harmony beneath that phrase. The return includes both the bright opening and its darkened answer.
transitions.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, Vivace, approach to the recapitulation and return of the opening phrase over C and A♭.

quote.text: The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I.
quote.source: London notebook, after his benefit concert on 4 May 1795; our translation

composer.background:
On 4 May 1795, Haydn gave a benefit concert at the King’s Theatre in London. The programme included his new D major Symphony, now numbered 104. Afterwards he entered the result in his notebook: “The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I. I made four thousand gulden this evening. Such a thing can only be done in England.” He was sixty-three, a wheelwright’s son who had spent most of his adult life wearing an Esterházy servant’s livery.

Haydn was born in Rohrau in 1732. His father made wheels, played the harp by ear and sang; his mother had worked as a cook. At about six, Joseph left home for schooling in Hainburg. By 1740 he was a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. Singing gave him a daily education in church music, though little instruction in composition. It also gave him chances to find a meal at performances outside the cathedral. When his voice broke and he was dismissed in 1749, another musician, Johann Michael Spangler, took him into his family’s crowded room.
